newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada bonds end stronger, outperform on dlr rally.
newsitem.headline: Canada bonds end stronger, outperform on dlr rally.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed much stronger on Thursday, although U.S. treasuries weakened as the biggest one-day rally in the Canadian dollar since 1995 drove prices higher, analysts said.

"What we're looking at is a pretty staggering performance in the Canadian dollar and that's where all the oomph is coming from. The monetary policy report today was friendly for the Canadian dollar," said Jeoff Hall, Canadian market analyst with Technical Data.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.40 to C$111.45 to yield 7.035 percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond fell 5/32 to yield 6.90 percent. The spread between the bonds narrowed to 14 basis points from 18 basis points at the close of trading on Wednesday.

The Canadian dollar rallied almost a one U.S. cent from Wednesday's close, prompting the Bank of Canada sell the currency to slow its rise. The currency rallied after the central bank said in its semi-annual monetary policy report that in the medium term the bank will need to shift to a less stimulative monetary policy. Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen also said in a news conference that he believes the underlying trend in the Canadian dollar is upwards.

"You almost never get situations where the Bank of Canada basically comes out and tells the market that they should be buying Canadian dollars, which was effectively the signal read from the Bank of Canada policy report," said Andrew Pyle, head of fixed-income research with ABN AMRO Bank Canada. "If you get that kind of move in the dollar, you don't want to be betting against Canadian bonds," Pyle said.

Canadian bonds pared earlier losses and strengthened following the release of the central bank report and comments from Thiessen. Pyle said volumes were heavy, with good two way flow and buying from both domestic and foreign sources.
In other prices, Canada's 10-year benchmark bond rose C$0.23 to C$103.50 to yield 6.501 percent. The U.S. 10-year bond fell 5/32 to yield 6.69 percent.
The negative spread between the two bonds widened to 19 basis points from 13 basis points at the close of trading on Wednesday.
The three-month cash T-bill traded with a yield of 3.02 percent against its U.S. equivalent which yielded 5.18 percent.
